x-m-m2-01.title: Making fractions that are finite decimals even though the denominator has a 3
x-m-m2-01.goal: Show with a counterexample that the claim 'if the denominator has a 3, it is always an infinite decimal' does not hold, and explain why such counterexamples occur.
x-m-m2-01.material: Jiho said, 'A fraction whose denominator has a 3 in it always turns out to be an infinite decimal.' How to read fractions: '9 over 12' means 9/12 (numerator 9, denominator 12). All the fractions below are written without being reduced.
x-m-m2-01.thinking.0: Finding a counterexample to a generalization
x-m-m2-01.thinking.1: Making examples that satisfy a condition yourself
x-m-m2-01.thinking.2: Reasoning out the condition for it to hold
x-m-m2-01.prereq.0: How to write a fraction as a decimal (division)
x-m-m2-01.prereq.1: The meaning of finite decimals and infinite decimals
x-m-m2-01.prereq.2: Divisors and multiples of natural numbers
x-m-m2-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the fractions that break Jiho's claim (counterexamples). A counterexample is 'a fraction whose denominator has a 3 but that is still a finite decimal.'
x-m-m2-01.s.s1.hint.0: To find a counterexample, you need a fraction that is 'a finite decimal even though the denominator has a 3.' What happens if you write each fraction as a decimal by dividing?
x-m-m2-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the denominator changes when each fraction is changed to its simplest form.
x-m-m2-01.s.s1.r.a: This choice noticed that even if the denominator has a 3, the denominator can change when the fraction is simplified together with the numerator.
x-m-m2-01.s.s1.r.b: Look back at whether you only noticed that the denominator has a 3, or whether you checked if the numerator 5 and the denominator 12 can be made simpler.
x-m-m2-01.s.s1.r.c: Check whether you changed 12/18 to its simplest form and then divided that fraction to write it as a decimal.
x-m-m2-01.s.s1.r.d: This choice found a case where the denominator 30 has a 3, but when simplified together with the numerator, the 3 disappears from the denominator.
x-m-m2-01.s.s1.r.e: Look at whether you felt it would be a finite decimal because the denominator 15 has a 5, and what happens to the 3.
x-m-m2-01.s.s1.explain: 9/12 = 3/4 = 0.75 and 15/30 = 1/2 = 0.5 had a 3 in the denominator, but when reduced the 3 disappears, so they are finite decimals. 12/18 = 2/3 = 0.666…, 5/12 = 0.41666…, and 8/15 = 0.5333… still have a 3 in the denominator after being reduced, so they are infinite decimals.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.prompt: Now make counterexamples yourself. The denominator b is a multiple of 3 and at most 60, and the numerator a is a natural number at least 1 and less than b. Make 3 fractions a/b that are finite decimals and have different values. (Fractions with the same value count only once.)
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.hint.0: First choose a denominator that is a multiple of 3, then change the numerator and divide to write it as a decimal.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.hint.1: For which numerators does the 3 disappear from the denominator when the fraction is simplified? Try the denominators 12 or 30.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The numerator is a natural number at least 1 and less than the denominator.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The numerator must be a natural number at least 1 and less than the denominator.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The denominator is a multiple of 3 and at most 60.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The denominator must be a multiple of 3 and at most 60.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.ok.c3: The fraction turns out to be a finite decimal.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.fail.c3: This fraction is not a finite decimal (written as a decimal, it goes on forever).
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.explain: Examples: 9/12 = 0.75, 15/30 = 0.5, 21/30 = 0.7, and 12/15 = 0.8 all have a denominator that is a multiple of 3 but are finite decimals. 5/12 and 7/15 cannot be reduced, so the 3 stays in the denominator and they are infinite decimals.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the fractions you made and explain why it is a finite decimal even though the denominator has a 3.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the fraction you chose in its simplest form and compare the denominator with the original denominator.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Look at which numbers the denominator of the simplified fraction is a product of.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you actually write the simplified form of the fraction you chose?
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain 'where the 3 went' by connecting it to the numerator?
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you say what the denominator of the simplified fraction must be like for it to be a finite decimal?
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.model.0: Reducing 9/12 gives 3/4. The 3 in the denominator is reduced away together with the numerator 9, and only 2×2 is left in the denominator, so it ends exactly at 0.75.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.model.1: Reducing 21/30 to lowest terms gives 7/10, and the denominator 10 is made of only 2 and 5, so it becomes the finite decimal 0.7. The 3 in the original denominator was reduced with the 3 in the numerator 21.
x-m-m2-01.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: An answer that directly states the condition 'only 2 and 5'

x-m-m2-02.title: Is 0.999… less than 1?
x-m-m2-02.goal: Revise your first judgment about the relationship between the repeating decimal 0.999… and 1 on the basis of two different pieces of evidence.
x-m-m2-02.material: 0.999… is a number with 9s that continue forever after the decimal point (the repeating decimal 0.9̇, read 'zero point nine repeating'). Look at the evidence one piece at a time and see how your thinking changes about how this number relates to 1.
x-m-m2-02.thinking.0: Revising a judgment according to evidence
x-m-m2-02.thinking.1: Comparing the conclusions of different methods
x-m-m2-02.prereq.0: The meaning and notation of repeating decimals
x-m-m2-02.prereq.1: Division for writing a fraction as a decimal
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.prompt: At each step, one more piece of evidence is revealed. Choose the judgment you can make with the evidence so far.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.hint.0: First think about which judgment is possible 'from only the evidence you can see now.'
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether your choice from an earlier step conflicts with the new evidence.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.info: We have not calculated yet. The more 9s you add one at a time, like 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, the closer it gets to 1. The number you get by continuing this process forever is 0.999….
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most reasonable guess right now about the relationship between 0.999… and 1?
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.after: A guess can change when there is new evidence. Let's test it with a fraction we already know.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A tiny bit less than 1. No matter how many 9s you add, it never reaches 1
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: 0.9, 0.99, and 0.999 are indeed all less than 1. But we have not yet tested whether we can treat the 'number that goes on forever' in the same way.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You may guess they are equal from the start. The reason is weak right now, so you need to test it with the next evidence.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Greater than 1. Since the 9s go on without end, it will eventually pass 1
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Think about the fact that only the places after the decimal point keep increasing. The whole-number part stays 0.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It is not a number, so it cannot be compared
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: It feels unfamiliar because it never ends, but an endless decimal like 1/3 = 0.333… is also a number.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Calculating 1/3 by division gives 0.333…. And 3 times 1/3 is 1. If you multiply each digit of 0.333… by 3, you get 0.999….
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: How does this evidence change your first guess?
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.after: This method relies on one case, 1/3. Let's see whether a completely different method gives the same conclusion.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: I lean toward equal to 1, because 1/3×3=1
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You used as your reason that two values obtained in different ways (1 and 0.999…) came from the same number.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Still less than 1. 0.333… is an approximation of 1/3, so multiplying by 3 falls a little short of 1
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This choice treats 0.333… as an 'approximation.' If the result of dividing 1/3 is 0.333…, think again about whether they are the same number written in different ways.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: I'm not sure yet. I want to check with another method too
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a careful attitude of not relying on only one piece of evidence.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: 1/3 and 0.333… are different numbers, so this evidence cannot be used
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: 0.333… is what you get from finding the value of 1/3 by division, so look for a reason why they would be different numbers.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Let x = 0.999…. Then 10x = 9.999…. Subtracting x from 10x gives 9.999… − 0.999… = 9, so 9x = 9 and x = 1. (Because the 9s go on forever, the decimal parts of the two numbers are exactly the same, so when you subtract, the decimal part becomes all 0.)
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now that you have seen both methods, how would you revise your first guess?
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.after: Look back at whether it was evidence, not a feeling, that changed your judgment.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Still less than 1. No matter how many 9s you add, it never reaches 1
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You applied the fact that 0.9, 0.99, … are less than 1 just as it is to 'one number that goes on forever.' Compare it with the value the two pieces of evidence point to.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Equal. Two different methods give the same conclusion, so it can be trusted
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This choice changed the judgment on the basis that two independent pieces of evidence agree.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Equal. 0.999… should be seen as one number that goes on forever
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This choice changed the judgment by taking the view of it as 'one already-determined number' rather than a 'process.'
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Greater than 1. Subtracting x from 10x gave 9, so x is bigger
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Read again the steps from 10x − x = 9 to 9x = 9, and check how the value of x was found.
x-m-m2-02.s.s1.reflect: At first, the feeling that 'no matter how many you add, it falls short of 1' is strong. But it is reasonable to change your judgment when one case (3 times 1/3) and another method (10x−x) point to the same conclusion. Look back at whether what changed your judgment was 'evidence' or 'mood.'
x-m-m2-02.s.s2.prompt: Minsu says, '0.999… is less than 1, because no matter how many 9s you add it never becomes 1.' Choose one of the two methods above and try to convince Minsu.
x-m-m2-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one of the two methods and show Minsu the calculation in order.
x-m-m2-02.s.s2.hint.1: In the last sentence, clearly write the relationship between 0.999… and 1.
x-m-m2-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Can you see every line of the calculation in the method you chose?
x-m-m2-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you answer Minsu's 'no matter how many you add, it never becomes 1' directly?
x-m-m2-02.s.s2.model.0: Minsu, 1/3 is 0.333…, and 3 times 1/3 is 1, right? 3 times 0.333… is 0.999…, so 0.999… and 1 are the same number.
x-m-m2-02.s.s2.model.1: Let x = 0.999…. Then 10x = 9.999…. Subtracting x from 10x leaves 9, so 9x = 9, which means x = 1. So 0.999… is equal to 1.
x-m-m2-02.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that convinces with a calculation

x-m-m2-03.title: Finding the mistake in a solution checked with x=1
x-m-m2-03.goal: Find the wrong line in a monomial calculation, then correct it while explaining why the value used for checking did not reveal the mistake.
x-m-m2-03.material: Seojin calculated (−3x²y)² ÷ 6xy² × 2x and wrote the solution below. To check it, Seojin substituted x=1, y=1, and since both the original expression and the answer gave 3, Seojin thought 'it is right.' (How to read: x² is 'x squared,' x⁴ is 'x to the 4th power,' and 6xy² is '6 times x times y squared,' and we divide by the whole 6xy² after ÷.)
x-m-m2-03.thinking.1: Judging the weakness of the checking method
x-m-m2-03.thinking.2: Finding values that reveal the mistake yourself
x-m-m2-03.prereq.1: Substituting numbers for letters to find the value of an expression
x-m-m2-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose one wrong line in Seojin's solution and check. (There may be more than one mistake.)
x-m-m2-03.s.s1.hint.0: Recalculate one line at a time to see whether each line follows correctly from the result of the line before it.
x-m-m2-03.s.s1.line.4: Substituting x=1, y=1 gives 3 for the original expression and 3 for 3x⁶, so the solution is right.
x-m-m2-03.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. In division, the exponents of the same letter are subtracted, not added. x⁴ ÷ x = x³, so this line should be (3/2)x³, and line 4 becomes 3x⁴. Line 5 is a problem too. x=1 stays 1 no matter what power you take, so even if the exponent is wrong, the value comes out the same.
x-m-m2-03.s.s2.prompt: Find (x, y) for which Seojin's answer 3x⁶ differs from the value of the original expression, and reveal the mistake. Make two pairs whose x values have different absolute values. (x and y are nonzero numbers. Calculate directly and check.)
x-m-m2-03.s.s2.hint.0: Substitute the values into the original expression and calculate first, then substitute the same values into 3x⁶ and compare.
x-m-m2-03.s.s2.hint.1: Think about why x=1, which Seojin chose, was weak, and choose an x that has a different nature.
x-m-m2-03.s.s2.fail.c1: x and y must not be 0 (if they are 0, you cannot find the value of the expression you divide by).
x-m-m2-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The value of the original expression and the value of 3x⁶ are different, so the mistake is revealed.
x-m-m2-03.s.s2.fail.c2: With these values the two values are the same, so the mistake is not revealed.
x-m-m2-03.s.s2.explain: If x=2, y=1, the original expression is (−12)² ÷ 12 × 4 = 144 ÷ 12 × 4 = 48, while 3x⁶ = 192, so they differ. x=1 or x=−1 gives the value 1 even when raised to a power, so a wrong exponent is not revealed.
x-m-m2-03.s.s3.prompt: Correct line 3, write the correct final answer, and explain in one sentence where it was wrong and why.
x-m-m2-03.s.s3.hint.0: If you write out x⁴ ÷ x directly (x×x×x×x ÷ x), how many are left?
x-m-m2-03.s.s3.hint.1: Carry the result of the corrected line into the next line and calculate through to the final answer.
x-m-m2-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Do the corrected line and the final answer connect correctly with each other?
x-m-m2-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give the reason that you must 'subtract,' not just that you 'added'?
x-m-m2-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you substitute x=2 yourself to check the new answer?
x-m-m2-03.s.s3.model.0: x⁴ ÷ x is not adding the exponents but subtracting them, which gives x³. So (3/2)x³ × 2x = 3x⁴ is the final answer.
x-m-m2-03.s.s3.model.1: In division you subtract the exponents, so x⁴÷x = x^3. Line 3 is (3/2)x³ and the final answer is 3x^4.
x-m-m2-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that writes exponents with ^ is also accepted
x-m-m2-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether you can say a solution is right just because the values of the expression came out the same, and recalculate each line from the previous line.

x-m-m2-04.title: Is there an a that makes the solution x<3?
x-m-m2-04.goal: Check with examples that the sign of a decides the direction of the solution of the inequality ax−6>0, and judge and explain the claim 'there is an a that makes the solution x<3.'
x-m-m2-04.material: In the inequality ax − 6 > 0, a is a number that has not been decided (read: 'a x minus 6 is greater than 0'). Sujin says, 'We can find an a that makes the solution x < 3,' and Minho says, 'There is no such a.' Let's gather evidence and judge whose statement is right.
x-m-m2-04.thinking.0: Collecting examples to reason out a rule
x-m-m2-04.thinking.1: Judging whether a claim is true or false
x-m-m2-04.prereq.1: Substituting numbers for letters to solve an expression
x-m-m2-04.s.s1.prompt: Put numbers in for a and solve ax−6>0, and make 2 pairs (a, k) with different a for which the solution has the form 'x<k.' k is the boundary value of the solution.
x-m-m2-04.s.s1.hint.0: Put one value in for a and solve ax−6>0 yourself.
x-m-m2-04.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the direction of the inequality sign differs when a is positive and when a is negative.
x-m-m2-04.s.s1.fail.c1: If a is 0, the inequality becomes −6>0, so you cannot talk about the shape of the solution.
x-m-m2-04.s.s1.ok.c2: For this a, the solution has the form 'x<k.'
x-m-m2-04.s.s1.fail.c2: For this a, the solution does not have the form 'x<k.' Solve it yourself.
x-m-m2-04.s.s1.ok.c3: k matches the boundary value (the x for which ax=6).
x-m-m2-04.s.s1.fail.c3: k is different from the x for which ax−6=0.
x-m-m2-04.s.s1.explain: If a=−2, then −2x−6>0 → −2x>6 → dividing both sides by −2 flips the inequality sign, giving x<−3. When a is negative, the solution has the form x<6/a, and the boundary value 6/a is negative.
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.prompt: Sujin says, 'There is an a that makes the solution x<3.' Judging by the evidence gathered above, which is most fitting?
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.hint.0: First sort out which direction the solution goes when a is positive.
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.hint.1: Solve to check for an a that gives a solution of the form 'x<3,' and then look at the sign of the boundary value.
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.o.a: There is no such a. If the solution has the form x<k, then k is negative
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.r.a: You looked at the sign of the boundary value 6/a and the direction of the solution together.
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.o.b: Choose a=2. 6÷2=3, so the boundary value is 3
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.r.b: You matched only the boundary value and did not check the direction of the solution. Solve it yourself to see which side the solution is on when a=2.
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.o.c: Choose a=−2. Dividing by a negative number flips the inequality sign, so it works
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.r.c: You pointed out that the direction flips, but you did not check what the boundary value is then.
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.o.d: It may be possible if you choose a as a fraction or decimal. We need to test more
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.r.d: The key is not the kind of number a is but the relationship between its sign and the direction of the solution. Solve with a fraction or decimal too.
x-m-m2-04.s.s2.explain: For the solution to have the form x<k, a must be less than 0, and then k=6/a is always negative. So you cannot make a solution like x<3 where k is positive. (If a>0, the solution has the form x>6/a, and if a=0, −6>0 is false, so there is no solution.)
x-m-m2-04.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Sujin why there is no such a. Include what the solution is when a is positive and when a is negative.
x-m-m2-04.s.s3.hint.0: Split into the cases where a is positive and where a is negative, and write the result of dividing both sides by a in each case.
x-m-m2-04.s.s3.hint.1: In the last sentence, answer 'is there an a that makes the solution x<3?'
x-m-m2-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the solution for when a is positive and when a is negative?
x-m-m2-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say why the boundary value cannot be 3 when a is negative?
x-m-m2-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about the case a=0?
x-m-m2-04.s.s3.model.0: If a is positive, then dividing both sides of ax>6 by a keeps the direction, so the solution has the form x>6/a. If a is negative, the direction flips and it is x<6/a, but 6/a is negative, so it cannot be 3. So there is no a that makes the solution x<3.
x-m-m2-04.s.s3.model.1: For the solution to have the form x<k, a must be negative, and then k=6/a is a value less than 0. 3 is positive, so it is impossible. If a is positive, the solution has the form x>6/a, and if a=0, there is no solution.
x-m-m2-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that even covers a=0

x-m-m2-05.title: Which notes do we need to find the prices?
x-m-m2-05.goal: When setting up simultaneous equations, judge whether the equations give different information, and make an equation that gives no new information yourself.
x-m-m2-05.material: We want to find out the price of one pencil, x원, and the price of one notebook, y원, at a stationery store. The owner showed us 5 notes that are true. Note A: 2 pencils and 3 notebooks cost 3,100원. Note B: 4 pencils and 6 notebooks cost 6,200원. Note C: A notebook costs 200원 more than a pencil. Note D: 6 pencils and 9 notebooks cost 9,300원. Note E: 5 pencils and 5 notebooks cost 6,000원.
x-m-m2-05.thinking.2: Making examples that give no information
x-m-m2-05.s.s1.prompt: When you choose two notes, choose all the pairs from which you can find both the price of a pencil and the price of a notebook.
x-m-m2-05.s.s1.hint.0: Rewrite the notes in the form 'pencils □ + notebooks □ = □원' and compare two notes side by side.
x-m-m2-05.s.s1.hint.1: Look for cases where multiplying every number in one note by some number gives another note.
x-m-m2-05.s.s1.r.a: Look back at whether you compared if the two notes give different information, or if one is the other multiplied by some number.
x-m-m2-05.s.s1.r.b: You paired two notes whose ratios of pencils to notebooks are different and got different information.
x-m-m2-05.s.s1.r.c: Check whether the amounts and counts both got bigger so it looks like new information, but is actually the same ratio.
x-m-m2-05.s.s1.r.d: You paired a note that gives a relationship in words with a note that gives a total and got different information.
x-m-m2-05.s.s1.r.e: You noticed that the two notes have different counts, so they give different information.
x-m-m2-05.s.s1.explain: Notes A, B, and D have the same ratio of pencils to notebooks, 2:3, and their amounts are the same multiples (1 times, 2 times, 3 times), so they repeat the same information. With only these notes, you cannot fix a single solution. If you pair notes with different count ratios (C, E), the two equations give different information, so the values are fixed. (Pencil 500원, notebook 700원)
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.hint.0: Multiply the number of pencils and the number of notebooks in Note A by the same number to make them bigger.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.hint.1: The total must be multiplied by the same number for everything to match. See how that multiplier relates to p.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of pencils and notebooks must be natural numbers that are at least 1.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The ratio of the counts is the same as Note A (2:3).
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The ratio of the counts is not 2:3, so it gives information different from Note A and the prices get fixed.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The total is the value of Note A scaled up by the same ratio.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The total does not match the value calculated from Note A.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain why you still cannot know the price of a pencil and the price of a notebook even after getting the new note.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the new note and Note A as equations, and look at the relationship between them.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about how many equations there are and how many possible prices there are.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say how many times Note A the new note is?
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you give at least two examples of possible prices?
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you write that 'there is only one equation'?
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.because.model.0: The new note is the same as Note A multiplied by some number, so it is not new information. In the end there is only one equation, so the price of a pencil and the price of a notebook are not fixed.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: An answer that even gives examples of possible prices
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.prompt: Make a 'new note' that does not fix the prices even when paired with note 가: buy p pencils and q notebooks for t won. Based on note 가, calculate and write the total t, and make 2 notes with different counts p. (Notes 가, 나, and 라 that already exist are not allowed.)
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.ok.c4: It is a new note different from 가, 나, and 라.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.fail.c4: If p is 2, 4, or 6, it is the same as an existing note 가, 나, or 라.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.explain: If the counts are a multiple of note 가's (a multiple of 2:3) and the total is the same multiple, there is no new information. For example: 8 pencils + 12 notebooks = 12,400 won, 10 pencils + 15 notebooks = 15,500 won. (4 pencils + 6 notebooks and 6 pencils + 9 notebooks already exist as notes 나 and 라.)
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.because.model.1: The new note is just note 가 made 4 times as big, so in the end there is only one equation. Pencil 500 won and notebook 700 won works, and pencil 800 won and notebook 500 won also works, so there are many possible prices.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.because.model.2: The new note is just note 가 multiplied by 2, so it is not new information. There is only one equation, so we can't know.
x-m-m2-05.s.s2.because.modelNote.2: An answer that states the relationship with multiplication

x-m-m2-06.title: How many lines pass through one point?
x-m-m2-06.goal: Using the relationship between the slope and y-intercept of a linear function through one point, make several lines that fit the conditions and judge what information is needed to fix a single line.
x-m-m2-06.material: The point P(2, 5) on the coordinate plane is the point whose x-coordinate is 2 and y-coordinate is 5. Make several lines y = ax + b that pass through point P, and think about what more information is needed to fix a single line. (There is no picture, and we work only with equations.)
x-m-m2-06.prereq.0: The meaning of the slope and y-intercept in the linear function y=ax+b
x-m-m2-06.prereq.1: Reading the coordinates of a point
x-m-m2-06.s.s1.prompt: Among the lines y = ax + b that pass through point P(2, 5), make 3 different lines whose slope a is greater than 0 and whose y-intercept b is a natural number. (You may write a as a decimal. Example: 1.5)
x-m-m2-06.s.s1.hint.0: To pass through point P, y must be 5 when x=2. If you put this into the equation, what relationship appears between a and b?
x-m-m2-06.s.s1.hint.1: Choose one b first and fit a to it, then check all the conditions (positive, natural number).
x-m-m2-06.s.s1.fail.c1: The slope a must be greater than 0.
x-m-m2-06.s.s1.ok.c2: The y-intercept is a natural number.
x-m-m2-06.s.s1.fail.c2: The y-intercept b must be a natural number.
x-m-m2-06.s.s1.fail.c3: When you put in x=2, y does not become 5, so it does not pass through point P.
x-m-m2-06.s.s1.explain: Putting x=2, y=5 into y=ax+b gives 2a+b=5. If b=1 then a=2, if b=2 then a=1.5, if b=3 then a=1, and if b=4 then a=0.5. If b=5 then a=0, and the slope is not positive. So there are only 4 lines in all that fit the conditions.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.prompt: We want to fix a single line through point P(2, 5). Choose all the pieces of information such that, with just one more of them, the line is fixed to a single one.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.hint.0: Change each piece of information into an equation or inequality in a and b.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check one by one whether using it together with 2a+b=5 fixes both a and b to single values.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.o.a: The line also passes through point Q(4, 9)
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.r.a: This choice checked whether one more point gives one more equation between a and b.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.o.b: The slope of the line is positive
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.r.b: Compare with the lines you made earlier to see whether the condition 'positive' fixes a single value or leaves many values.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.o.c: The y-intercept of the line is 3
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.r.c: This choice checked whether knowing the value of the y-intercept fixes a to a single value through the relationship between a and b.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.o.d: The line also passes through point R(2, 8)
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.r.d: Did you compare the x-coordinate of R with the x-coordinate of P? Think about whether the line through the two points can be written in the form y=ax+b.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.o.e: The slope of the line is 2
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.r.e: This choice checked whether knowing the value of the slope fixes b to a single value in 2a+b=5.
x-m-m2-06.s.s2.explain: The condition of passing through point P is just one equation, 2a+b=5, so you need one more equation. Using point Q(4, 9) gives 4a+b=9, and from the two equations a=2, b=1. If the y-intercept is 3, then b=3, so a=1. If the slope is 2, then a=2, so b=1. The condition that the slope is positive does not fix the values to a single one. R(2, 8) has the same x-coordinate as P, so the line through both points is perpendicular to the x-axis and cannot be written in the form y=ax+b.

x-m-m2-07.title: Fixing a solution that judged a linear function from a table
x-m-m2-07.goal: Learn that when judging from a table alone whether a relationship is a linear function you must also look at the increase in x, then fix the error in the solution and apply it to a new table.
x-m-m2-07.material: We want to find out from a table whether the relationship between x and y is a linear function (y=ax+b, a≠0). I will read the table in words. When x is 1, 2, 3, 5, y is 5, 8, 11, 17 in order. (Table: x | 1 2 3 5 / y | 5 8 11 17)
x-m-m2-07.thinking.2: Applying the fixed criterion to new data
x-m-m2-07.prereq.0: The meaning of the linear function y=ax+b (a≠0)
x-m-m2-07.prereq.1: Reading the relationship between two quantities shown in a table
x-m-m2-07.s.s1.prompt: Below is one student's solution. Choose one wrong line.
x-m-m2-07.s.s1.line.0: When x increases by 1 from 1 to 2, y increases by 3 from 5 to 8.
x-m-m2-07.s.s1.line.1: When x increases by 1 from 2 to 3, y increases by 3 from 8 to 11.
x-m-m2-07.s.s1.line.2: When x goes from 3 to 5, y increases by 6 from 11 to 17.
x-m-m2-07.s.s1.line.3: The increases in y are 3, 3, 6, which are not constant, so it is not a linear function.
x-m-m2-07.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong. In the third interval, x increased by 2, not 1. If the increases in x are different, you must not compare only the increases in y. Checking with (increase in y) ÷ (increase in x) gives 3, 3, 6÷2=3, all equal, so it is a linear function (y=3x+2).
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.prompt: How should this solution be fixed? Write the correct way to judge and the conclusion for this table.
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.hint.0: Think about how to connect the increase in y and the increase in x in each interval so that you can compare the intervals.
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write how the conclusion differs when the compared values are all the same and when they differ.
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.placeholder: Example: If we also look at the increase in x, ...
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you also write the increase in x for each interval?
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you change the criterion from 'the increases in y are the same' to '(increase in y) ÷ (increase in x) is the same'?
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you check yourself that the conclusion matches the values in this table?
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.model.0: In each interval you have to divide the increase in y by the increase in x. 6÷2=3, so all three intervals are equal at 3, which means it is a linear function.
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.model.1: x did not increase by 1 but by 2, so the rate of change is 6÷2=3. The slope is constant at 3, so it is the linear function y=3x+2.
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that even finds the equation
x-m-m2-07.s.s3.prompt: Use the fixed method to judge the tables below. Choose all the tables in which the relationship between x and y is a linear function (y=ax+b, a≠0). (Read each table as an 'x: …' line and a 'y: …' line.)
x-m-m2-07.s.s3.hint.0: For each interval, write (increase in y) ÷ (increase in x).
x-m-m2-07.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether that value is the same in all intervals, and think about what happens if the value is negative but still the same.
x-m-m2-07.s.s3.r.a: Look back at whether you also checked the ratio of the increases in the last interval, where x does not increase by 1.
x-m-m2-07.s.s3.r.b: Compare the value you get by dividing the increase in y, 4, by the increase in x, 2, in the last interval with the values of the earlier intervals.
x-m-m2-07.s.s3.r.c: Check whether you saw that the increases in y grow as 3, 5, 7, and whether the increase in y is the same while x increases by 1 each time.
x-m-m2-07.s.s3.r.d: You confirmed that even if y decreases, it is a linear function if the value divided by the increase in x is the same.
x-m-m2-07.s.s3.explain: For a, the slopes are 3, 3, 9÷3=3, all 3 (y=3x−5). For d, the slope is constant at −4÷2=−2 in each interval (y=−2x+7). For b, it becomes 3, 3, 4÷2=2, so it differs, and for c, it keeps changing as 3, 5, 7.
x-m-m2-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write which interval of the table each line compares, and check in the table whether the conditions of those intervals are the same.
x-m-m2-07.s.s1.hint.1: For each interval, write the amount x changed and the amount y changed, and check whether each line's conclusion comes from those records.
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.model.2: Dividing the increase in y by the increase in x gives 3, 3, 3, so it can be seen as a linear function.
x-m-m2-07.s.s2.modelNote.2: An answer that used the ratio of increases for all three intervals

x-m-m2-08.title: What do we need to be sure it is a parallelogram?
x-m-m2-08.material: Suppose that for a quadrilateral ABCD, each of the following conditions is given by itself, one at a time. (Opposite sides are the sides facing each other, and diagonals are the segments joining opposite vertices. There is no picture.)
x-m-m2-08.thinking.0: Judging whether a condition is sufficient
x-m-m2-08.thinking.2: Telling apart conditions that make it hold
x-m-m2-08.prereq.0: The meaning of parallelogram and trapezoid
x-m-m2-08.prereq.1: Terms such as opposite sides and diagonals
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the conditions from which you can say that quadrilateral ABCD must be a parallelogram from that condition alone.
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether there is a figure that satisfies each condition but is not a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.o.a: One pair of opposite sides is parallel, and the other pair of opposite sides has equal length
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.r.a: This is a condition that splits 'parallel' and 'equal length' across different pairs of opposite sides. Look for a figure that satisfies this condition but is not a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.o.b: Both pairs of opposite sides have equal lengths
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.r.b: This choice checked whether the condition that opposite sides are each equal in length determines a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.o.c: The two diagonals have equal length
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.r.c: Think about whether there are figures with equal diagonals other than rectangles.
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.o.d: The two diagonals bisect each other
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.r.d: This choice checked whether the condition that the diagonals meet at each other's midpoints determines a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.o.e: One pair of opposite sides is parallel and equal in length
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.r.e: This choice connected the condition that two parallel sides are also equal in length to the properties of a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.explain: b, d, and e are all conditions that make a parallelogram. For a and c, the isosceles trapezoid is a counterexample. An isosceles trapezoid has one pair of opposite sides parallel, the other pair of sides (the legs) equal in length, and equal diagonals too, but it is not a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.prompt: Make a quadrilateral that satisfies the condition 'one pair of opposite sides is parallel and the other pair of opposite sides has equal length' but is not a parallelogram. Let the lengths of the two parallel sides be a (top side) and b (bottom side), and the length of the other two equal sides (legs) be c, and make 2 with different shapes. (Swapping the top and bottom sides counts as the same shape.)
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.hint.0: Choose different lengths for the two parallel sides, and compare the leg length with the difference between the two side lengths.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.hint.1: Think of the two legs as each taking half of the difference between the top and bottom sides, and use the fact that the legs must be longer than that.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.fail.c1: The lengths must be greater than 0.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The two parallel sides have different lengths, so it is not a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.fail.c2: If the two parallel sides have the same length, it turns into a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The legs are long enough, so such a trapezoid can be made.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The legs are too short, so such a quadrilateral cannot be made (they must be longer than half the difference of the two bases).
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.explain: Example: A trapezoid with top side 4, bottom side 10, and legs 5 is not a parallelogram because its parallel opposite sides have different lengths. If the legs are too short, the lines coming down from the two ends of the top side cannot reach the bottom side, so it cannot be made.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain why the quadrilateral you made is not a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Recall the condition that the parallel opposite sides must meet for a figure to be a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Substitute the values of a and b that you made and write them out.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: The top side and the bottom side ...
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain using the lengths you made as numbers?
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you state the condition that 'the parallel opposite sides must be equal in length'?
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you tell apart why this quadrilateral is a trapezoid but not a parallelogram?
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.because.model.0: The top side 4 and the bottom side 10 are parallel but have different lengths. In a parallelogram the parallel opposite sides must be equal in length, but these are not, so it is not a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.because.model.1: a=4 and b=10, so the two parallel sides are not equal in length. Even if one pair of opposite sides is parallel, if their lengths differ, it is not a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.goal: Tell apart the conditions that guarantee a quadrilateral is a parallelogram from those that do not, and make a counterexample yourself for the conditions that do not guarantee it.
x-m-m2-08.s.s1.hint.1: Draw a quadrilateral that satisfies the condition you chose by setting the lengths yourself, and check whether its remaining sides and angles match the properties of a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.because.model.2: The top and bottom sides are parallel but their lengths are different, 4 and 10, so it cannot be a parallelogram.
x-m-m2-08.s.s2.because.modelNote.2: An answer that wrote the conclusion as 'cannot be'

x-m-m2-09.title: If all the angles are equal, are the figures similar?
x-m-m2-09.goal: Judge with examples for which figures the generalization 'if all corresponding angles are equal, the figures are similar' holds and for which it does not.
x-m-m2-09.material: Jian thought like this: 'Two triangles whose three angles are each equal are similar, right? So rectangles, whose four angles are all equal at 90°, must all be similar too.' (Similar means that one figure can be enlarged or reduced by a fixed ratio and laid exactly on top of the other figure.)
x-m-m2-09.thinking.0: Judging the range in which a generalization holds
x-m-m2-09.prereq.0: The meaning of similarity and the ratio of similarity
x-m-m2-09.prereq.1: The meaning of rectangle and rhombus
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.prompt: Write a rectangle that is not similar to the 3 by 4 rectangle (width 3, height 4), using width c and height d. Make 3 with different width : height ratios. (Swapping width and height counts as the same shape.)
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.hint.0: Think about what the ratio of the side lengths must be for the figures to be similar.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.hint.1: Make one rectangle each with a ratio different from 3×4, and check that even if you swap width and height it is not 3 : 4.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.fail.c1: The lengths must be greater than 0.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.ok.c2: The width : height ratio is not 3 : 4.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.fail.c2: The width : height is the same as 3 : 4, so the rectangles are similar.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.ok.c3: Even if you swap width and height, it is not 3 : 4.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.fail.c3: If you swap width and height it becomes the same as 3 : 4, so the rectangles are similar.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.explain: Examples: 3×5, 5×5 (a square), and 2×7 are all rectangles with four 90° angles, but their width : height ratios differ from 3 : 4, so they are not similar. 6×8 is 2 times 3×4, so it is similar.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.because.prompt: Explain why they are not similar even though all four angles are equal at 90°.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.because.hint.0: Write what relationship between the lengths is needed to lay one figure on the other after enlarging or reducing.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.because.hint.1: Explain by comparing one rectangle you made with 3×4.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the width : height ratios with numbers?
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Did you connect 'even if the angles are equal' with 'because the ratios of the sides are different'?
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.because.selfAssess.2: Did you use the rectangle you made as an example?
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.because.model.0: A rectangle has four 90° angles, but if the ratio of width to height differs, it does not lay on top of the other even after enlarging or reducing. To be similar, not only the angles but also the ratios of the corresponding side lengths must be equal.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.because.model.1: Doubling 3×4 gives 6×8, but 3×5 has a different width-to-height ratio, so the shape does not fit however you enlarge or reduce it. Equal angles alone do not make figures similar.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.because.modelNote.1: An answer that compares with numbers
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.prompt: Then, from the following, choose all the pairs of figures for which you can say 'they are always similar as long as all corresponding angles are equal.'
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.hint.0: Work out whether, once the angles are fixed, you can change the ratio of the side lengths freely.
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.hint.1: Imagine whether you can draw two figures with equal angles so that one is long and thin and the other is flat.
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.o.a: Two parallelograms whose four angles are each equal
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.r.a: Check whether, even if the angles are equal, you can freely change the ratio of the lengths of two neighboring sides.
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.o.b: Two triangles whose three angles are each equal
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.r.b: This choice checked whether it is a figure whose shape is fixed to a single one once the angles are fixed.
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.o.c: Two rectangles whose four angles are each equal
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.r.c: Recall the counterexample you just made yourself.
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.o.d: Two rhombuses whose four angles are each equal
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.r.d: This choice checked whether, when all four sides have equal length, the shape is fixed just by fixing the angles.
x-m-m2-09.s.s2.explain: For a triangle, once the angles are fixed the shape is fixed to a single one, so they are similar. For a rhombus, all four sides are equal, so once the angles are fixed the shape is fixed, so they are similar. For rectangles and parallelograms, the ratio of two neighboring sides can change, so even with equal angles they may not be similar.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.because.model.2: When enlarged, the width and height must change by the same factor, but if it is not 3:4, they do not fit on top of each other.
x-m-m2-09.s.s1.because.modelNote.2: An answer that explained with the same scale factor and 3:4

x-m-m2-10.title: The probability of exactly one head with two coins
x-m-m2-10.goal: Check with evidence that the cases counted by 'number of heads' do not happen equally often, and revise your first judgment about probability.
x-m-m2-10.material: Toss two fair coins at the same time, once. If you describe the result only by the number of heads, there are 0, 1, or 2. Look at how your thinking about 'the probability of exactly 1 head' changes with evidence.
x-m-m2-10.thinking.0: Revising a judgment according to evidence
x-m-m2-10.thinking.2: Comparing theoretical probability and experimental results
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.prompt: At each step, one more piece of evidence is revealed. Choose the judgment you can make with the evidence so far.
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.hint.0: First think about which judgment is possible 'from only the evidence you can see now.'
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the new evidence changes the assumption of your earlier choice.
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.info: If you split the possible results only by the number of heads, there are three: '0 heads,' '1 head,' and '2 heads.'
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most fitting guess for the probability of exactly 1 head?
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.after: Let's check with the next evidence whether the method of counting by 'number of heads' is fine.
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is 1/3, because it is one of three results
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This guess assumes that the three results happen equally often. That assumption has not been checked yet.
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is 1/2, because heads or tails seems to be half and half
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This guess carries over the feeling for one coin to two coins. The reason still needs more thought.
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We cannot tell. We must first check whether the three results happen equally often
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is an attitude of asking 'do they happen equally often?' before deciding a probability.
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It is 1/4, because there are two coins, so 1/2 × 1/2
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.r.d: 1/2×1/2 is the probability of one specific result, like 'both coins are heads.' Think about how many ways there are to get exactly 1 head.
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.info: If you distinguish the coins (a 100원 coin and a 500원 coin) and write ordered pairs, there are 4 results: (heads, heads), (heads, tails), (tails, heads), (tails, tails). Each coin is equally likely to show heads or tails and they do not affect each other, so these 4 results happen equally often. The cases with exactly 1 head are (heads, tails) and (tails, heads).
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: Seeing this evidence, how would you change your guess?
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.after: When we changed what we count, the probability changed. Shall we see whether this calculation matches actual results?
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Keep it at 1/3, because the number of heads is only three possibilities: 0, 1, 2
x-m-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: There is no reason that '0, 1, and 2' happen equally often. Count how many ways the case of 1 head is made up of.
